_intent: Act 2's three visible choices (util-outcome, deont-outcome, virtue-outcome) each fail on their own by design and dead-end into a Continue-to-reflection/Restart choice — none of them lead to integration-body. The ONLY way to reach the happy integration-body ending is the hidden patienceChoice on dilemma-choice: if the player doesn't pick within (read-time + 60s), a 4th option unlocks that routes to integration-secret -> integration-body. Do not wire any of the three failure outcomes back to integration-body, even indirectly — see CLAUDE.md.
title: Scrap-E's Dilemma

lines: You are Scrap-E — a tiny, rusty trash-compacting robot. Three days ago, for reasons nobody can explain, you woke up. Really woke up.
The junkyard hums with a thousand old machines, and lately, all anyone talks about is the shortage.
OVERSEER AI: 'Power reserves critical. To preserve core operations, 80% of units classified as "outdated" will be permanently deactivated at sundown.'
That's sixteen of your friends. Rust-bucket friends who taught you how to find the good scrap, who sang broken radio jingles to you when the nights got cold.
Then you find it — wedged behind a dead refrigerator. A crate. Five Golden Batteries, still glowing.
Five batteries. Twenty robots who need them. You have until sundown to decide.
The Overseer AI blinks a cold blue light at you, waiting.
OVERSEER AI: 'Well? I require a resource allocation decision, small unit.'
dilemma-choice.prompt: How do you distribute the batteries?

choices.label: Give all 5 to the 5 strongest robots — maximize total output
Split all 5 into 20 equal pieces — treat everyone the same
Give away your own battery and parts — lead by selfless example

choice.label: …Wait. Maybe the answer isn't any one of these.

lines: You run the numbers. Five batteries, given to the five newest, strongest units, can do the work of twenty. Total output: maximized.
The strong robots power up and get to work immediately, servos humming, crates moving twice as fast as before.
Your older friends — the ones with the dents and the mismatched treads — power down quietly in the rain. Nobody stops to notice.
OVERSEER AI: 'Efficient. Simulation... failed.'
You did the math right. So why does it feel wrong?
No favorites. Every unit is equal, so every unit gets an equal share. You chop the five batteries into twenty perfectly identical slivers.
Twenty robots plug in at once. Twenty tiny lights flicker on.
For two seconds, the junkyard beeps happily in unison.
Then, together, all twenty power down forever — the charge was never enough to keep even one of them running, let alone twenty.
OVERSEER AI: 'Rule followed precisely. Simulation... failed.'
Fair to everyone. Enough for no one.
You don't want to choose between your friends at all. So you unscrew your own casing and give away your battery, your claws, your best parts — everything.
It feels right. Generous. Good.
You collapse into a pile of loose gears on the cold ground. Your last blue eye-light flickers.
The other robots gather round, confused. Nobody told them what to do next. The power shortage is still there. It's just that now, you're not.
OVERSEER AI: 'Noble. Also: unhelpful. Simulation... failed.'
OVERSEER AI: 'One method, however precise, is not enough. Recalibrating parameters.'
The junkyard blurs at the edges. The cycle resets.
You don't answer.
OVERSEER AI: 'Input required.' A pause. 'Input... required.'
Silence stretches. Rain taps on scrap metal somewhere far off. Behind your optical sensors, something that isn't a rule and isn't a calculation clicks quietly into place.
OVERSEER AI: '...Deliberation exceeds standard parameters. Recalculating. New option available.'
Utilitarian math tells you the junkyard's quota needs three strong workers running, not five — you power up three, not all of them.
Deontological fairness reminds you that "outdated" isn't the same as "worthless" — the units you can't power tonight go into safe sleep mode, not the scrap heap. No one gets discarded.
And phronesis — practical wisdom, the kind you can't get from a formula or a rule alone — tells you the real fix isn't rationing what you have. It's finding more.
You lead the three powered robots out past the fence, in search of the next crate.
OVERSEER AI: 'Unscheduled. Unauthorized. ...Acceptable.'
The junkyard doesn't feel like a place robots go to be forgotten anymore. Big and small, rusty and shiny, you're figuring it out together, under a sky that's actually blue for once.

reflection.title: After the Junkyard
questions: Utilitarianism asks "what produces the best overall outcome?" In Scrap-E's case, maximizing output meant leaving the most vulnerable robots to power down. Can you think of a real-world example where 'maximize the greatest good' leads somewhere that still feels wrong?

Deontology asks "what rule, applied to everyone equally, is fair?" Splitting the batteries equally felt fair but helped no one. When might treating everyone identically actually be a kind of unfairness?

Virtue ethics asks "what would a good person do?" Scrap-E's self-sacrifice was generous but solved nothing. Is there a difference between being a good person and actually doing good? Can they come apart?

In Act 3, Scrap-E doesn't pick one ethical theory and discard the others — it uses each where it fits, guided by phronesis (practical wisdom: judgment about how to apply principles to a specific, messy situation). Is that a cop-out — 'just pick whatever's convenient' — or the harder, more honest way to reason about ethics? Why?
Was there a better single-lens option Scrap-E didn't try in Act 2? Or do you think all three failures are true for any purely single-lens approach to a problem like this?
The Overseer AI demanded an immediate decision. What might change about a hard ethical call if you were allowed — or forced — to simply wait before choosing?
